ChatGPT Ads is replacing two manual bid caps with average cost targets. Here's what changes for new campaigns, existing campaigns and API partners, and when.

The ChatGPT Ads platform is replacing two manual caps, the maximum bid (Max Bid) and maximum CPC (Max CPC), with average cost targets that advertisers can set as part of their advertising campaign strategy. This is according to an OpenAI help document on the topic of bidding and pricing that was updated on their website Thursday.

Beginning Nov. 9, advertisers creating a conversion campaign, which they are using to hit a specific cost per conversion, get Target CPA in place of Max Bid; likewise, advertisers creating a click campaign beginning Nov. 9 also have the option to use Target CPC. Max Bid and Max CPC will no longer apply to existing campaigns from Jan. 1, 2027.

From Nov. 18, a Max Bid or Max CPC value that an API partner sends through the old fields to create a campaign or change an ad group’s bid type becomes an average target, not a maximum.

OpenAI’s bidding page describes Target CPA and Target CPC as average cost goals rather than limits on each bid. Target CPA is the average of what an advertiser wants to spend on a conversion (such as a purchase or a lead) and Target CPC is the average for a click. In both cases, a single click or conversion may cost more or less than your target, and you may end up paying more or less on average.

For click campaigns, the page compares the new option with the cap it replaces:

“While Max CPC caps individual bids, Target CPC lets our system bid above or below your target in individual auctions, aiming to deliver as many clicks as possible from your budget while working toward your desired average CPC.”

The warning on this page is about a possible restriction on delivery when the target is set below recent performance. An example shows how they calculate a $40 actual CPA using $400 in ad spend and 10 attributed purchases. It points out that if a $20 Target CPA is set it does not mean that the system will be able to deliver purchases at a $20 cost. Additionally, the amount spent by a campaign may fall short of the full budget due to overly restrictive targets or poor conversion data.

This page says the bidding goal and the billing event type are two different settings and therefore, a Target CPA campaign can be optimized for conversions while being charged for clicks or impressions, which depends on how the campaign is being billed.

In August Brooke Osmundson reported that Microsoft would cease to offer Max CPC on new non-portfolio campaigns using a strategy such as Target CPA and Target ROAS beginning Oct. 1. However, existing campaigns and portfolio bid strategies may continue to use it. Microsoft’s official reasoning behind the change is that the setting can interfere with their bidding systems’ ability to perform optimizations toward performance objectives.

API partners are getting their own Target CPA and Target CPC fields, and the old Max Bid and Max CPC fields change behavior on Nov. 18. The bidding page says partners can adopt the new fields once they’re available but doesn’t give a date for them.

OpenAI suggests that the legacy fields be replaced with the new fields starting Nov. 18. Legacy fields will stay active until the end of December; however, if you utilize a field to create a campaign or convert an ad group’s bidding strategy, it switches to Target CPA or Target CPC and the value becomes counted as an average cost instead of a maximum bid.

On Jan. 1, 2027, legacy fields will be deprecated. As such, the page advises partners to have all integrations updated prior to this date.

OpenAI’s bidding page also explains how the price of a winning ad is set:

“The final winning auction bid sets the price you pay.”

That rule applies across all bidding strategies, including existing Max Bid and Max CPC campaigns, the page says.

The company’s advertiser basics page described a relevance-weighted, second-price auction when I read it on Nov. 5. However, that wording is gone after an update, and the page now uses the same pricing rule as the bidding page.

The basics page also still says advertisers set a maximum bid at the ad-group level, and it recommends that CPC campaigns start with a maximum bid of $3 to $5 per click. In April, I covered Digiday’s report that an early version of the ads manager showed CPC bids in that range to some pilot advertisers.

The Maximize results page is still telling advertisers who are required to operate within a bid limit that if they have to do so without an automated process, they can do it using manual or advanced bid controls. Its setup steps say to select Manual: Max bid to use a different strategy. Also, the bidding page gives the old Maximize results strategy a new name, Intelligent bidding.

With Max Bid and Max CPC, advertisers have the ability to limit how much they will bid in each auction. With Target CPA and Target CPC, it is the advertiser who sets both a budget and an average cost; then it is up to the automated bidding systems to set individual bids. Some individual clicks or conversions could come in at higher costs than the targets.

As OpenAI suggests, advertisers should consider setting their targets based upon recent actual CPA or CPC averages. In addition to reviewing the overall spend of the campaign as well as results (clicks, conversions), advertisers should also monitor the actual average cost per click or conversion as the campaign continues to learn. Advertisers who buy through API partners should find out which bid fields those tools use after Nov. 18, since a legacy max-bid value sent to create a campaign will count as an average target.

Target CPA and Target CPC are available in Ads Manager beginning Nov. 9, with advertisers able to move their campaigns from this date forward. The legacy API bid field changes behavior on Nov. 18 and is going away Jan. 1, 2027, which marks the end of Max Bid and Max CPC for those who have yet to switch.

There is no information on OpenAI’s bidding page as to what will be the target of a campaign that is still using Max Bid or Max CPC after the caps retire. By switching prior to retirement, the advertiser is able to set its new target at the time of the switch.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

US stock market futures leaned lower as Fed governor Christopher Waller said that he would support hiking interest rates by 25 basis points at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on Dec. 9. At the time of writing, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.4%.

His decision, he added, would not be swayed by lower-than-expected inflation data. The October prints of the US Consumer Price Index (CPI) is due for release at 8.30 am Eastern time on Tuesday. It is expected to show a month-on-month increase of 0.3% versus September when the increase was 0.6%, pushed higher by rising fuel costs.

“While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC’s policy rate at our December meeting,” Waller commented in a speech at the Bank of England Watchers Conference in London.

While CPI is particularly sensitive to fuel-price volatility, Waller also flagged high readings from the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, known to be the Fed’s “preferred” inflation gauge and which he confirmed was the “measure targeted by the FOMC.”

“Let’s just say it. September’s inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining,” he said, referring to PCE rising 0.5% month-on-month and 3.7% year-on-year, respectively.

gta vi takes over miami with six real-life cars built by west coast customs

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

from a pink-and-purple sports coupe to a police-liveried supercar, the fully drivable lineup turns fictional automotive excess into something with actual horsepower.

Rockstar Games has brought six vehicles from Grand Theft Auto VI out of the screen and onto the streets of Miami, enlisting Los Angeles-based West Coast Customs to transform fictional designs into fully drivable machines. The project arrives ahead of the game’s November 19 release, translating some of its most recognizable automotive creations into physical vehicles. From classic American lowriders to contemporary supercars, the collection recreates the exaggerated personalities that have long defined the franchise’s approach to car culture.

The six vehicles retain their fictional brand names, distinctive silhouettes and elaborate finishes, with modifications extending well beyond their exterior appearance. Each has been presented alongside its digital counterpart, revealing how closely the real builds follow their virtual references. Photographs also place the collection at recognizable Miami landmarks, including Herzog & de Meuron’s 1111 Lincoln Road parking structure and the Miami Marine Stadium. The locations connect the actual city with Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional interpretation of Florida’s coastal metropolis.

Among the six creations developed by Rockstar Games in collaboration with West Coast Customs, the Grotti Cheetah draws on the proportions of classic Italian supercars, with a low-slung body, sculpted side intakes and a naturally aspirated 4.9-liter V8 engine. The customization workshop finishes the vehicle with a gradient paint treatment, lowered suspension and custom leather upholstery. The Invetero Coquette takes a more contemporary direction, pairing a 6.2-liter V8 with a striking pink-and-purple camouflage exterior. Meanwhile, the Progen Emerus embraces track-inspired engineering, combining a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 with aerodynamic bodywork, an oversized rear wing and a bright orange interior.

American automotive culture provides the references for the Albany Buccaneer and Albany Manana. The former reinterprets a 1960s lowrider with candy-green metallic paint, gold wheels, air suspension and zebra-patterned interior details. The Manana follows a different tradition, adopting the dramatically elevated stance of a donk-style custom car, complete with oversized wheels, blue bodywork and gold accents. Completing the lineup is the Pegassi Tempesta, a V10-powered supercar dressed in the fictional Vice Beach Police Department’s black-and-white livery. Apparently, even law enforcement gets a supercar in Leonida.

The project reflects the close relationship between Grand Theft Auto’s visual identity and real-world automotive customization. Throughout the series, Rockstar Games has developed fictional manufacturers and vehicles that borrow recognizable proportions and styling cues from established brands while exaggerating their defining characteristics. Translating these designs into functional machines requires more than reproducing their shapes. Paint finishes, wheel proportions, suspension setups and interior materials become essential to preserving the identity of each vehicle beyond the screen.

The resulting collection also highlights the influence of Miami’s automotive culture on the fictional world of Vice City, from extravagant lowriders to brightly colored performance cars. By placing the vehicles in the same urban environment that inspires the game, Rockstar Games brings its digital references back to their physical origins. With Grand Theft Auto VI scheduled to launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19, the six builds offer an unusually tangible preview of its universe, where even the most improbable designs appear perfectly at home on the road.

“1970” follows 13-year-old Draško, who — after being abandoned by his parents — runs away with the rebellious 16-year-old Eržika. Drifting from place to place, swept up amid a roiling climate of anti-war protests, rebellion, free love, wild rock concerts, drugs and decadent parties, his desperate journey home becomes an awakening of heartbreak, loss and freedom. Related Stories ‘Star Trek’ 60th Anniversary Celebration Hits Rome MIA Market With Iconic Franchise at 'Crossroads’ After Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger

The film is written and directed by Lungulov, who shares a producing credit with Snezana van Houwelingen. It’s produced by This and That Productions (Serbia), Papa Films (Serbia), Mirage Film (Hungary), Samsa Film (Luxembourg) and PomPom Film (Croatia), with financing and support from Film Center Serbia, the Hungarian National Film Institute, Film Fund Luxembourg, the Croatian Audiovisual Center, Film Fund Vojvodina and Creative Europe MEDIA.

Speaking to Variety in Thessaloniki, Lungulov explains that while his period drama is set more than 50 years in the past, “it is a story about today.”

“The film takes us to a time when young people believed they could change the world — something we seem to have forgotten,” the director says. Pointing to recent events in his native Serbia, where after two years of struggle, a student protest movement ousted longtime strongman Aleksandar Vučić last month, Lungulov says that “that possibility came incredibly to life again.”

The Belgrade-born director, who studied filmmaking in New York, is best known for “Here and There,” which won the Best NY Narrative Award at Tribeca in 2009 and was Serbia’s submission for the foreign-language Oscar that year. The film, which contrasted the adventures of an enterprising young Serbian in New York with the experiences of an aging New Yorker in Belgrade, was praised by Variety’s Ronnie Scheib as a “laid-back character study [that] accrues small epiphanies with patient care, its mordant Eastern European humor tempered by a gentler sense of postwar absurdity.” His 2014 follow-up, the tragicomedy “Monument to Michael Jackson,” premiered at Karlovy Vary.

Lungulov’s last film was the 2023 documentary “A Fleeting Dream,” which followed the rock band Yu Grupa — a long-running musical act that, coincidentally, was formed in 1970. His latest will also incorporate documentary elements, with “1970” utilizing a mix of “real and fake home movies, newly shot 16mm and digital footage,” he says. “It is a film based on my own memories, and I wanted to create the hero’s inner world, his memories and the atmosphere of 1970 through the film’s internal language.”

Mirroring the political climate of that time, with raucous anti-Vietnam War protests greeting Nixon’s visit to Yugoslvaia, Lungulov notes that his two young leads — Andrija Femić, who plays Draško, and Lilla Gregus, who plays Eržika — were both “very active in the student movement” that brought down Vučić. At the time of filming, Gregus was a 22-year-old student at the Academy of Arts in Novi Sad, the Serbian town whose railway station disaster in 2024 jumpstarted the protest movement.

On one occasion, Lungulov himself joined the young actor and her fellow students at a demonstration after a rehearsal for “1970.” It’s that echo of the past in the present day, he says, that makes his film so timely.

“I feel this story is about today — young people searching for their voice in a hopeless world and refusing to be broken by bullying authorities, which feels like our last hope in today’s scary times,” he says. “And the Serbian students brought that hope back to us in Serbia, and perhaps to the world.”

The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

GTA 6 is now available for preload if you have a spare 212GB

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Beat the rush so you’ll be ready to play when the game unlocks on November 19.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

With its release just nine days away, Grand Theft Auto VI is now available for preloading on Xbox Series X|S and PlayStation 5 in most regions around the world. This means that once you pre-order the game, you'll be able to fully install it to your console's drive ahead of the November 19th release. Given GTA 6's huge 212GB file size and reported pre-release sales already around 8 million copies, pre-loading would certainly help you avoid any rush.

Publisher Rockstar Games staggered the game's digital preloading schedule, starting yesterday at 7 PM EST for Xbox Series X and S owners. If you have a PS5 or PS5 Pro console, preloading opened at midnight today local time (November 10) across all regions. For those with a physical copy of GTA 6, it will start shipping and arrive at retail stores on November 12th. A box in the code will allow you to preload the game as soon as it arrives.

GTA 6's reported 212GB file size could pose an issue for many users. Even if you own a 2TB PS5 Pro, it's going to use a lot of your space. And if you have a standard 512GB Xbox Series S console, the game will take up more than half of the approximately 362GB of usable storage. Preloading will thus allow users to make sure their storage is organized and ready for the download, something that will be doubly important if there's a day-one patch.

If you're on Xbox and pre-ordered GTA 6, you can start preloading by going to the Microsoft Store, searching for Gran Theft Auto VI and selecting install. You can also pre-download by enabling "Keep My Games & Apps Up to Date" in the Settings > System > Updates section. On PS5, find and select the preload option on the PlayStation Store's GTA 6 page. You can set it to automatically download the game by going to your Game Library, selecting the GTA 6 pre-order and toggling the Auto-Download setting on.

Give yourself plenty of time, as a 212GB could take hours to load depending on your connection speed. To get started, you'll first need to order the game: Grand Theft Auto VI costs $80 for the Standard Edition and $100 for the Ultimate Edition, on the Xbox or PlayStation stores, along with retailers including Amazon and Walmart.

SHANGRAO, China, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Jinko Holdings Limited ("Jinko Holdings" or the "Company") (NYSE: JKS), today announced that its majority-owned principal operating subsidiary, Jinko Solar Co., Ltd ("Jinko Solar"), a global leader in clean energy technology, was invited to attend the Business 20 (B20) Summit on November 9, 2026, in Washington, D.C. As the only photovoltaic company invited, it participated as a core member of the Energy Task Force, engaging in discussions with leaders from globally renowned companies, international organizations, and business associations on energy issues. This marks the 11th consecutive year that Jinko Solar has been invited to attend the B20 Summit.

The theme of the 2026 U.S. B20 Energy Task Force's recommendations was "Powering global growth through secure, abundant, and affordable energy supply and infrastructure." It calls on Group of Twenty (G20) leaders to collaborate with the private sector to mobilize various forms of investment, support technological innovation, enhance universal access to energy, accelerate the improvement of the global energy system, and achieve long-term sustainable prosperity for both the environment and the economy. It also calls for strengthening global energy security through resource investment and infrastructure development, ensuring an adequate energy supply through a diversified and inclusive energy mix, and addressing the surging demand for electricity driven by artificial intelligence (AI) and the industrial sector by advancing grid modernization.

The B20 Energy Task Force serves as the core platform for energy recommendations from the G20 business community, focusing on key issues such as global energy security and infrastructure development. The recommendations will be submitted to G20 leaders for consideration. As a core member of the Energy Task Force, Jinko Solar contributes its industry expertise and practical experience to discussions on global energy challenges and policy recommendations.

Drawing on its frontline industry practice, it has turned its experience in affordable green energy supply, solar and storage synergy, and the integration of computing and power into actionable projects. GOP senator withholds support for Thune as leadership showdown looms

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., isn’t ready to back John Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader. He and other Republicans want specifics on how Thune, or another contender, would get work done as Democrats prepare to take control.

FIRST ON FOX: A Senate Republican isn’t ready to support Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., to stay as the top Republican as the GOP’s leadership elections fast approach.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., in an interview with Fox News Digital, argued that whoever would be the next to lead the Senate GOP and earn his vote in the process needed to lay out a plan on how Republicans would pass key agenda items heading into the lame-duck session of Congress before Senate Democrats take control in January.

Thune plans to run again for another term as the GOP leader, but Scott and a cohort of others want to delay Tuesday morning’s leadership elections to debrief after stunning losses across the board on Election Night. Whether he’ll support Thune for another term depends on his pitch.

SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said he won't support John Thune for Senate GOP leader without a plan to pass key agenda items. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I don't want to put the cart before the horse," Scott said. "I mean, I think the first step is what do we want to accomplish? And then anybody, including John Thune, if they want to be that, the first thing I have to say is, ‘Do they want to do that?’"

"If that's not what they want to accomplish, then why would we elect them? But if that's what they want to accomplish, then tell us why they're the best at it," he continued.

Senate Democrats flipped the upper chamber with wins in red states across the country, clinching a 54-seat majority that could grow even more depending on the outcomes of outstanding races in Mississippi and Alaska.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

That gives Republicans little time with a trifecta in government to ram through key remaining agenda items before Democrats officially take over.

Thune still plans on running for leader, too, despite the grumbling among Republicans. He said on Monday after lawmakers returned to Washington that he expected a "very engaged conversation" ahead of the leadership election.

"We'll see where it goes from there, but, yeah, I'm running for leader, and I think it's important that we have that discussion, and we will," Thune said.

Scott said that he wants the candidates to be "specific" on how they can balance the budget and pass a slew of legislation, including a stock trading ban for lawmakers, permitting reform, the National Defense Authorization Act and the SAVE America Act.

SCHUMER TANKS POPULAR INSIDER TRADING BAN IN DEM EFFORT TO DERAIL REPUBLICAN'S AGENDA AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks during a Senate Republicans press conference at the U.S. Capitol on June 2, 2026, flanked by Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., and Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)

All of that, he said, would be a show that Republicans are listening to voters after getting pummeled in the midterms.

"Back home, they don't care about anything other than do we make their lives better," Scott said.

Thune is so far running unopposed for the top job — Scott reiterated that he had no interest in running again, trying twice for the gig, once against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022, and in 2024 when Senate Republicans were searching for McConnell’s replacement.

When asked if he would like to see someone else jump into the fray, Scott said, "Oh, I wouldn't do that to anybody."

Scott and Sens. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., Ted Budd, R-N.C., John Kennedy, R-La., and Mike Lee, R-Utah, all signed onto a letter demanding that Republicans meet before holding their leadership elections and delay voting until they have a full debrief on the midterm losses and what comes next.

They’re joined by Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., who called for the elections to be delayed but did not sign onto the letter pushing leadership for a meeting.

When asked how long he’d like to see the leadership elections delayed, Scott said, "I think this first step is how long is it gonna take us to agree on what our path should be?"

"If we can get that done quickly, then we can, you know, have elections after that," he said. "And then people that want to run with that agenda in mind, saying they believe in that agenda and will work hard to get that agenda accomplished, then that's how we would decide how we vote."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

We tested dozens of earbuds: These 8 are the best for noise-cancelling

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Over-ear headphones are everyone's usual go-to solution for blocking out the world. And listen, I get it. You couldn't pry my Sony WH-1000XM6s out of my cold, dead hands. But honestly, as much as I love them, carrying around a clunky pair of headphones on the go isn't always ideal. I want a pair of headphones to tuck in my pocket that will still block out noise. That's the promise of the best noise-cancelling earbuds.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Every top brand has its own take on ANC earbuds, each with a unique style and a plethora of features. Since you can't possibly try all the latest earbuds, the Mashable team has taken on the task of reviewing the best ANC earbuds for you. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

While there are plenty of audio brands that provide good sound quality and noise cancellation, the best of the best ANC earbuds can elevate your listening experience. Not only do they offer phenomenal ANC, but they also make music and podcasts sound better. Trust us — on the right pair of earbuds, Olivia Rodrigo's latest album will have you singing along even louder, somehow.

Earbuds usually aren't as comfortable as over-the-ear headphones. I know this well, as I've found many pairs of earbuds that just plain don't fit in my ear. Others are downright uncomfortable. Once again, Bose offers the most comfortable headphones and earbuds. However, Bose and Sony aren't the only brands out there. That's why we set out to test the best the market offers and see what makes a great pair of wireless earbuds.

Read our full review of the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds.

Anyone who needs earbuds to get the world to near quiet: Not everyone will want to shell out over $300 for earbuds, but for folks who budget for having the best of the best, the Sony WF-1000XM6 are what we recommend.

Their combination of excellent sound quality, noise cancellation, and design is unmatched by any other option currently available, making them the best overall earbuds we've tried.

If the asking price on a pair of earbuds is $330, it better have little to no faults — thankfully, that's exactly the case with the Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds.

Going into our testing, we expected the XM6 earbuds to sound great — Sony products typically do. We didn't expect them to sound the best out of every Sony earbud and headphone we'd previously tested. Whether we listened to Stravinsky's "The Firebird" or a live performance from Daft Punk, these earbuds highlighted the richness, clarity, and layers of each track we played on them.

What surprised us even more than the excellent sound quality, however, was the active noise cancellation. Sony products generally have pretty good ANC, but not necessarily the best of the best. With the XM6 earbuds, they're making a strong play to change that reputation: the ANC felt at least on par with the Bose QC Ultra 2 earbuds, which had been the best we'd experienced on a pair of earbuds. Sony even shone over the Bose when we tested the ANC without streaming any audio: the slight hiss of the ANC at work is more detectable on the Boses than the Sonys.

Sony also upgraded the design of the case and earbuds between the XM5 buds and the XM6s. Though the case feels like more of an aesthetic change, the earbuds take on a more oval-like shape than the rather circular XM6s, helping them sit more flush and naturally in the shape of the ear. The result? One, the earbuds cause noticeably less fatigue after hours of wear. Two, the tighter seal helps provide more passive ANC.

The short of it? These earbuds aren't cheap — but we totally get why.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd gen) earbuds.

If your earbuds always fall out, look no further: For earbuds that have noise cancellation that performs better than many over-ear headphones, you'll want to look no further than the second-generation QuietComfort Ultra earbuds. Though they're not drastically different from their predecessor (first-gen owners should skip this release), they provide some of the best ANC and all-day wear available on the market.

We were big fans of the first-generation QC Ultra earbuds, thanks to their rich sound profile, class-leading ANC, and comfortable fit. With the second-generation buds, Bose didn't exactly reinvent the wheel — but it did make some minor improvements that helped make an already standout pair of earbuds even better.

For starters, the QC Ultras come with a wireless charging case, which helps make the case for shelling out $299 for them. They also include Bose SpeechClarity tech, which we noticed helped voices sound noticeably clearer on calls than with the first-generation buds. The ANC also got a boost, somehow blocking even more than the first-generation buds. Though less exciting, they also added an earwax guard to the bud tips, which did help in the cleaning process.

While there were no dramatic improvements, we appreciated that Bose understood you don't want to mess with a good thing. In this case, that's the stability band/ear tip combo that makes wearing them snugly for long periods of time feel possible without any discomfort, a robust sound profile that can make all genres sing out of the box, and overall, a premium earbud that feels like it's worth its price tag.

Read our full review of the Panasonic Technics EAH-AZ100.

The sound-obsessed: Audiophiles who wants the best of the best sound quality should look to the Panasonic Technics AZ100 earbuds. They've flown under the radar since their December launch, but they have unmatched sound clarity. Multiple Mashable team members found that they stood out, even compared to flagship over-ear headphones.

There are earbuds sounds good enough, and there are earbuds that sound so good they make you understand what audiophiles are always going on about. These fall into the latter category. Simply put, if you're looking for the best earbuds for audiophiles, it doesn't get better than the AZ100.

Thanks to the earbuds' Magnetic Fluid Driver, they're capable of producing sound closer to the original recording than most consumer audio devices. In his review of the earbuds, Mashable's Timothy Beck Werth wrote that these earbuds let you appreciate all the layers of your favorite tracks, concluding, "[they] deliver richer, fuller, more detailed sound than any earbuds I've ever tested. The only buds I've tried that achieved similar clarity and sound separation were next-gen in-ear monitors that used ultrasound technology."

In addition to sounding incredible, these earbuds also have excellent (and adjustable!) active noise cancellation that stands up to other premium options. They support lossless audio via LDAC codec, multipoint connection with up to three devices, 10 hours of battery life per charge — and they come with a metal case and accent, lending them an overall more premium experience.

So why aren't they our top pick? Well, these earbuds can cause some soreness after a few hours wear, so they're not a great option if you like to wear earbuds for long stretches of time (like during a work day). They also rarely dip down from their $299 price tag, making them a less accessible option for most people.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort earbuds.

Folks with a medium earbuds budget that want maximum returns: If you want good-quality sound but don’t want to spend over $200, the Bose QuietComfort is an affordable answer to the brand’s line-up. They’re focused on a great fit, as they not only come with multiple ear tips but multiple bands that can be changed out on the earbuds for a better fit on the crest of your ear.

The accompanying app lets you adjust audio levels, but you won’t need to, as these earbuds make all your music sound better. They’re reliable, have a long battery life, and are sure to please the pickiest of audiophiles.

I’ve sung the praises of the QuietComfort Ultra, but Bose’s latest earbuds, the entry-level QuietComfort, are also fantastic, especially with their under-$200 price tag. Even after adjusting the ear tips and bands, I didn’t find the fit on these quite as secure as the Ultras. However, my colleague Bethany Allard, who also tested the QuietComfort earbuds, said they were the best earbuds that have ever fit her.

The QuietComfort’s sound quality is just phenomenal. With these earbuds, listening to Ethel Cain’s A House in Nebraska immersed me in the orchestrations. When Brick House by The Commodores came on, the earbuds elevated the snappy drum beats so that I may have been listening live.

The noise cancellation on the QuietComfort earbuds isn’t as sophisticated as the Ultras; I found they had more sound leakage and that classic ANC buzz when I was in noisy environments. However, the ANC on these is still great, especially in quiet spaces.

One tiny beef I have with the Bose QuietComfort earbuds is that they require a different app than the standard Bose one. This is annoying if you’re an existing Bose user and need to download another app; plus, this earbud app just isn’t as good as Bose’s flagship app.

All in all, these are a solid pair of headphones that, for $179, are an unbeatable value.

Read our full review of the Apple AirPods Pro 3.

Apple fans who appreciate ease: If you're an iOS user who wants to avoid dealing with an auxiliary app, Apple AirPods Pro 3 are your best bet. They have impressive noise cancellation and seamlessly connect to iOS systems. To pair them to your iPhone, just open the charging case. Need to go hands-free? The AirPods will announce your texts to you.

iPhone users have long been fans of the AirPods Pro line, and for good reason. The earbuds offer excellent quality ANC and connect with Apple devices with record speed and consistency.

In the Pro 3 buds, Apple's upped the ante. In his review, Mashable contributor Adam Doud noted that the earbuds noise cancelling ability gave him a "personal cone of silence," even in the midst of a busy conference. Doud found the sound profile was flat, but balanced. Considering many earbuds these days can leave bass heavy, this is a huge plus in Apple's direction. To round out the basics, these earbuds also come with eight hours of battery life per charge, putting them on par with other earbuds leading in this category.

Apple didn't stop there, though. These earbuds can perform live translation across six different languages, making them an excellent travel companion. And for anyone who likes to track their workouts but not so much that they're ready to invest in a fitness tracker, the built in heart rate monitor is an added boon.

Read our full review of the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2.

Runners, cyclers, gym rats: Tired of your earbuds falling during exercise? Even more tired of blaring music at the gym killing your vibe? The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 kill two birds with one stone, offering an exercise-forward design with an ear hook that can still be used as an in-ear earbud with ANC.

It can be hard enough to motivate yourself to exercise without a pair of earbuds adding friction to the process.

The Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 are designed to fit seamlessly into your workouts and elevate them. After testing them, we found the Mashable Choice Award winner was more than worthy. The ear hook/in-ear combo design is unique and can take some adjusting to get used to, but once you do, these buds aren't going anywhere. While providing top-notch ANC isn't the highest priority on these earbuds, the ANC you do get is workable, especially if you're (most likely) listening to music.

The thoughtfulness of the design extends beyond the ear hook. Tactile on-ear controls are perfect for not accidentally switching songs during reps, IPX4 water and dust resistance is great for keeping the buds safe from sweat, the expansive battery life means you aren't too likely to run out of battery mid-workout, and the built-in heart rate monitor is a nice fitness tracking bonus to an all-over well-rounded pair of earbuds.

Sure, these probably won't be your daily driver in every situation, but for workouts, these are sure to get the job done.

College students, teenagers, or anyone looking for cheap earbuds that don't suck: If you're on a tight budget but still want to enjoy noise cancellation, the Anker Soundcore Life P3i earbuds offer a surprisingly solid performance. Don't expect elite ANC, but these affordable earbuds don't require too much of a sacrifice in sound quality.

We're going to start with the major hitch of these earbuds: switching between devices sucks. They don't have multipoint pairing, and if you want to use them with your phone after using them with your laptop, you have to manually disconnect them (or, in our experience, sometimes outright unpair them) with your laptop first. It's easily their biggest flaw, and where we most obviously felt their price point during testing.

With that out of the way, these earbuds still have a lot going for them. For starters, they cost $50 and can often be found on sale for even less. Though inexpensive, these earbuds are comfortable to wear all day, have a custom equalizer in the app plus 21 presets (we're fans of the Treble Booster), customizable touch controls for each earbud, and a battery life that outdoes the Apple AirPods Pro. You won't have extras like spatial audio, and the ANC leans on background hiss more than premium models, but not terribly so.

For a pair of $40 earbuds, we're impressed. We recommend them for anyone who doesn't want to shell out $100 plus for a pair of noise-cancelling earbuds.

Read our full review of the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special earbuds.

Side sleepers, restless sleepers, or the sleepless: Whoever needs to hear this: there are more comfortable earbuds to sleep in than the ones you'd wear out and about during waking hours. Good sleep earbuds have much flatter profiles while still staying in your ear easily overnight. The feature set on the Soundcore Sleep A30 Special buds makes them the absolute best our team has tried, and our top pick for noise-cancelling sleep earbuds.

When it comes to sleep earbuds with noise cancellation, the pool is limited, as in the only real options are from Soundcore. That said, this wasn't a recommendation by process of elimination situation.

Soundcore makes legitimately great sleep earbuds, with comfortable interchangeable ear and wing tips, excellent battery life that lasts for several nights on end with the charging case, sleep tracking features, integrated meditations from Calm, a built-in alarm, and a host of soundscapes on the companion app. Touch controls work effectively for snoozing alarms or switching listening modes, as do sleep detection features that automatically switch your audio preferences as you drift off.

Considering competitors charge higher prices for similar feature sets (minus the noise cancellation), the Soundcore earbuds are also a great value, relatively speaking. They may be too much of an investment for some, but if you're persistently waking up due to noisy neighbors or a snoring partner at night, these earbuds are likely worth considering.

All noise-cancelling headphones, including earbuds, have some passive noise cancellation. While over-the-ear headphones naturally block out noise by wrapping around the ears, earbuds don't block sound as effectively. Instead of covering your ears, wireless earbuds deliver sound directly into the ear canal to drown out other noises. They rely more on active noise cancellation (ANC) to reduce environmental noise.

ANC is an electronic process within the headphones. Internal microphones listen to your surroundings and then invert the sound, effectively canceling it. Sometimes, with noise-cancelling headphones and earbuds, you'll hear a slight buzzing or humming in the background, and that's the ANC at work. The best ANC earbuds shouldn't have this buzzing, however.

We focus on wireless earbuds in this guide, because historically, wired noise-cancelling earbuds haven't really existed. Until recently, that is. In late September, Bose dropped its Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds for $99 — we'll be evaluating them as a contender for a spot on this list, but Deputy Shopping Editor Miller Kern had positive initial thoughts on their performance.

Mashable shopping reporters, editors, and contributors regularly test new noise-cancelling earbuds and headphones from brands such as Apple, Beats, Bose, Dyson, JBL, Marshall, Sonos, and Sony.

Samantha Mangino, Bethany Allard, and other Mashable team members tested each pair of earbuds in this guide over several weeks. Similar to how we test the best noise-cancelling headphones, here's what we considered:

Though we always consider this feature when testing headphones, we paid extra attention for the purposes of this guide. We made sure to wear these earbuds indoors and outdoors, while someone was trying to speak to us, and went about our usual workdays.

Though this category can be extra subjective due to different user preferences and head and ear sizes, we evaluated comfort and ear fatigue for each model we tested. We also examined how adjustable headphones will suit different wearers, including whether they come with extra ear tips in varying sizes.

While testing the earbuds, we listened to music across a variety of genres with our standard Mashable headphone playlist, songs we're very familiar with, and podcasts to see how they perform in different audio settings.

With the above features in mind, we compared the earbuds' price points to determine which products are worth it. For premium headphones, we evaluated if they came with interesting extra features through their companion apps, or particularly smart designs. We also made sure every pair checked the basic boxes, like having decent battery life.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for three years at Mashable.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

Trump's Supreme Court majority faces looming threat after Dem Senate takeover: 'Stuck'

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito discusses the origins of originalism, his upbringing and the court’s unique position among other branches of government on ‘Life, Liberty & Levin.’

Republicans' loss of the U.S. Senate in the midterm elections could have far-reaching consequences for President Donald Trump's judicial agenda, threatening his ability to reshape the federal courts and raising new questions about the future of the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority.

With Democrats set to take control of the Senate in January, Republicans face a shrinking window to confirm Trump's judicial nominees, while any future Supreme Court vacancy could leave the president dependent on Democratic support to install a replacement.

"Lawless Lawfare" author Alex Swoyer told Fox News Digital, the election results could leave the court's oldest conservative justices with a difficult decision over when to retire.

"It's likely the justices — mainly Justices Thomas and Alito — are stuck on the high court for at least six more years with Democrats taking control," Swoyer said. "Both in their late 70s, I could see why they may want to retire now, midterm."

Supreme Court Justices Samuel Alito, Clarence Thomas and Brett Kavanaugh share a laugh while waiting for their opportunity to leave the stage at the conclusion of the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the US Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Justice Clarence Thomas, 78, and Justice Samuel Alito, 76, are the court's two oldest conservatives, making their retirement decisions particularly consequential as Republicans prepare to lose control of the Senate.

Alito, however, confirmed to Fox News on Thursday that he has no plans to retire and is committed to serving through at least the current Supreme Court term, with the justices expected to wrap up their major decisions in late June or early July.

Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"While Senate Republicans were able to confirm Justice Barrett in a one month timeframe in 2020, I don't think this GOP Senate has that same work ethic or ability to push a nominee through ahead of January," Swoyer said.

"I think conservatives would like to see them try; however, a judicial nominations expert told me the Senate work calendar ahead of the holidays would not afford them enough time," she added. "While a five week window seems workable, it doesn't appear like Senate Majority Leader John Thune would have the support to usher such a move at this time."

The stakes extend beyond the Supreme Court. As of Nov. 8, the federal judiciary had 28 vacancies, with 16 nominees awaiting confirmation for current and future vacancies, leaving Republicans with limited time to advance Trump's picks before Democrats take control of the Senate.

Zack Smith, a senior legal fellow for courts and the Constitution at the Heritage Foundation, said Republicans should focus on confirming Trump's remaining lower-court nominees before their majority expires.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, celebrating her 20th anniversary on the bench, is photographed in the West conference room at the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., on Friday, August 30, 2013 (Nikki Kahn/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

"The top priority for Senate Republicans right now should be confirming the lower federal court judges President Trump has already nominated. It will take all Senators showing up and doing their part. But it is possible," Smith told Fox News Digital.

"As for the Supreme Court, even if a Justice announced his or her retirement today, it could prove difficult to get a replacement confirmed before the end of the current Senate, although Senate Republican leadership has indicated a willingness to try. However, neither Justice Alito nor Justice Thomas has indicated any plan to retire."

The uncertainty surrounding Thomas and Alito echoes the debate over the late liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who resisted calls to retire before the 2014 midterms despite concerns that Republicans could take control of the Senate and complicate efforts to confirm an Obama-appointed successor.

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION

Republicans won the Senate in 2014 and, two years later, refused to consider Obama's Supreme Court nominee, Merrick Garland, following Justice Antonin Scalia's death. Trump won the 2016 election and appointed Neil Gorsuch to Scalia's seat in 2017.

Ginsburg remained on the bench until her death in September 2020, just weeks before the presidential election. Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett to replace her, and the Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Barrett days before Election Day.

Barrett's confirmation gave conservatives a 6-3 majority on the Supreme Court, a balance that has shaped some of the nation's most consequential legal decisions, including the 2022 ruling overturning Roe v. Wade.

Warhammer Survivors Review - Bringing A Tank To The Mad Forest

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

I spent hours carving through termagants with a chainsword and watching their sprites explode into a viscera of gems before Warhammer Survivors finally clicked. It wasn’t until I unlocked the tank and started rolling through the Ork Stronghold, turning pixels into paste beneath the running gear, that I finally got it: this isn’t just a Vampire Survivors reskin. It’s a Warhammer power fantasy that lets you unleash an orbital bombardment on the poor denizens of the Imperial Bastion, doling out the Emperor’s duty while you rummage through chests to turn garlic—ahem, Shield of Faith—into the Emperor’s Wrath.

Warhammer Survivors almost reminds me of those old ‘00s crossover games, like Peggle Extreme, where child-friendly unicorns are coupled by Half-Life headcrabs as blood drips from their horns. It’s unashamedly Vampire Survivors underneath the prettier UI, boltguns, and fusil-cannons, but once you push through and begin to unlock the more experimental Warhammer weapons, it becomes its own beast.

If you’ve played Vampire Survivors or its myriad clones, you’ll know the core gameplay loop: kill enemies, collect gems, acquire weapons, kill more enemies. Warhammer Survivors is familiar but a little more sluggish, with its hulking brutes clad in Space Marine armor. But even as someone who isn’t embroiled in the tabletop side—with passing knowledge thanks to Dawn of War and Boltgun—it just felt cooler. The whip was always a bit flimsy. Serviceable, but you toss it aside the second you get something better. Turn that whip into a chainsword, and suddenly I can’t let go of the thing.

Warhammer Survivors is split into two campaigns with their own progression systems, so it’s not just 40K on offer. Age of Sigmar is more familiar, with its high-fantasy tropes that throw you straight into a stage brimming with rats and other vermin. But this was another concept I just wasn’t sold on, as passing through the realmgate from one universe to the other was a bit of a slog at first. The two campaigns share so much DNA in their starting weapons, and both have the exact same passives, that it took a while to appreciate what each had to offer as I was forced to retrace my steps. Again, once I got past the first few hours, the two began to diverge with truly unique weapons and stages that felt every bit as rewarding to experiment with—it’s just a shame you have to push through to truly appreciate it.

So much of Warhammer Survivors pays homage to Games Workshop’s miniature wargame, such as paint buckets that unlock new characters and a bit box menu to view all your weapons in. But one of the most inventive ways that it captures the feeling of placing tiny figurines onto a board is how unlocking new weapons works. Not every character can use every item, so you’ll gradually build a squad with their own unique arsenal. There are mages brandishing the shield of faith, grenadiers lobbing grenades, Space Marines carving with the chainsword, and a tank. Just a tank. Can you imagine having a tank in the Mad Forest? That’s what this game is.

It’s a crucial part of what makes Warhammer Survivors feel less like a reskin and more like its own distinct entry into the Survivors genre canon, but I’m not sure it lands. Using weapons like the shield of faith, which is Auroch Digital’s answer to garlic, is a lot less satisfying when it’s permanently off-center or lagging behind as your troops get separated by the horde. It turns the satisfying gameplay loop of becoming an unstoppable powerhouse into a fiddlier game of wrangle-the-squad. It doesn’t matter so much when evolutions are brought into the fold, and suddenly you have five unstoppable heretics deleting everything in sight, but it’s another hurdle that slows the pace and makes the early moments of a game less rewarding.

And while Warhammer Survivors does eventually diverge and become its own experience, the early game is so similar to Vampire Survivors, with blatant reskins of weapons and passives, that I was even able to use Vampire Survivors guides to figure out evolutions. So much of the initial crawl is carried by the sheer cool factor of Warhammer’s aesthetic. It’s a bit of a shame that the early game is tantamount to a texture pack, imagining what Vampire Survivors weapons would look like in Warhammer, rather than imagining what Warhammer weapons would look like in a survivor game. Especially given how much better the game gets when Auroch Digital finally starts taking more ambitious swings.

After years of waiting, this forgotten chapter is finally ready for an explosively stylish return.

With that being said, the pixel art, thematic UI, and retro synthwave fantasy music are all a step above Vampire Survivors. Hearing the war drums clang as I marched along the rivers of molten realmstone in the Bloodwind Spoil, hurling poison knives and tempest axes, had me completely enthralled by the Age of Sigmar universe. As much as it owes to Vampire Survivors, it feels rooted in Warhammer, right down to the Orks launching a Waaagh! that summons massive, enraged hordes, to the end-of-stage boss encounters like the enormous Norn Emissary tyranid in place of the Grim Reaper.

Warhammer Survivors takes a while to sound the horn, and spends so much of its early hours awkwardly stuck between itself and the Vampire Survivors foundation. Some of its ideas fall flat, and it doesn’t always reach the heights of its inspirations, but once it sheds its roots and embraces the outlandish theocratic tyranny of tanks rolling on Poxwalkers, it becomes a moreish sandbox where smashing together miniatures just to see what happens is endlessly entertaining—and thankfully, it won’t get you kicked out of the hobby shop.

Warhammer Survivors Review: Late to the Game But Packed With Bullets

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The budget-priced Warhammer Survivors brings a variety of unlocks and franchise fanservice, but feels a little unevolved for the bullet heaven genre.

Story isn’t a crucial component here, but there is some fun Warhammer lore to collect.

It’s unsurprisingly quite similar to Vampire Survivors with weaker feedback overall, but there’s a lot to unlock and some surprise elements further into the game.

Could have served as a DLC, but larger sprite sizes, greater map detail, and some visual surprises manage to outdo vanilla Vampire Survivors.

OST is repetitive and uninteresting, audio feedback is lacking.

Warhammer can seem intimidating from afar, but the many video games minted from Games Workshop’s tentpole wargaming IP have brought countless new fans into the fold. There have been over a hundred such video games thus far, with few as easy to pick up and play as Auroch Digital’s Warhammer Survivors, a new fully licensed riff on Poncle’s Vampire Survivors, the bullet heaven action-roguelite dynamo that set the standard for the subgenre.

Imprinting Warhammer’s extensive lore, dark oddball humor, and formative tropes onto Poncle’s dopamine-juicing treadmill sounds like an easy swish. And, while perhaps feeling a tad too similar to justify its own SKU, Warhammer Survivors delivers an eminently playable counterpart to its vampiric predecessor. Anyone fond of both the subgenre and the Warhammer brand will find a considerable distraction here, but the game needs another pass for polish, and I wish it simply added more to the formula.

Like Vampire, Warhammer Survivors dispenses with any attempt at storytelling and tosses you into the action with a choice between two campaigns: 40,000 or Age of Sigmar (read as: sci-fi or fantasy). Both “worlds” hold a troupe of 20 unlockable heroes with dozens of weapons and relics to stack and track and synergize. Pick a toon and map, mark up any mods, then head off to war, directing the non-reptilian part of your brain to other affairs, like a low-stakes Netflix series or comedy podcast.

If you’ve somehow managed to sidestep the bullet heaven survivors genre until now, let’s briefly dig into the basics. Each level presents an infinitely scrolling pixelated map, with hordes of spawning enemies swirling into your hero as you work to avoid contact damage and projectiles, all while hoovering up XP, coins, and power-ups. Maxing out the XP bar delivers a choice of various active and passive items, with select pairings producing a scripted synergy that overpowers the basic weapon at hand. You choose where and when to move, but attacks are always automatic and constant.

Elite minibosses materialize every few minutes and drop a treasure chest on defeat. Open it and endure a dizzying Vegas-styled jackpot celebration and stack of cash. Money accumulates over multiple runs and feeds a metaprogression menu that boosts your basic stats, so even failure leaves something behind in the tip jar. You’ll lose early and often, but those buffed stats eventually slacken the resistance and ticks up your win-to-loss ratio.

Ten minutes deep into a run, you'll be eradicating dozens of mobs in a blink with a kill-count into the tens of thousands, multicolored damage numbers snapping like popcorn, utterly incoherent in the fracas.

Warhammer Survivors’ metaprogression and a few of its power-ups are reskinned from Vampire Survivors outright. Still, most bullet heavens crib freely from one another—Vampire Survivors is itself a riff on Korean mobile game Magic Survival—and there are some fun irreverent hat tips to the wargaming pastime here. You can collect paint pot relics, wield Nuln Oil and dice as weapons, and some other cheeky references set the game apart from Vampire Survivors’ 8-bit horror theming.

Beyond that, the hero objectives, Extremis Bosses, and faction traits in Warhammer Survivors are all wholly unique and excellent additions to the format. Some heroes are unusual indeed and tap directly into the lore, like Knight-Commander Pask and his massive Leman Russ Battle Tank, and Commissar Sebastian Yarrick with his Power Klaw. Like any other weapons, these can be unlocked and equipped later on, regardless of your initially selected hero.

That plays into the game’s squad mechanics, though I found them somewhat frustrating in action. Essentially, if your chosen hero cannot equip a granted weapon, someone from the pool will be conscripted and added to your team to wield it, which can get clumsy to control.

For instance, the straight-shooting boltgun is hard enough to aim properly when it’s in your own hands, but having to angle its shots from a teammate trailing behind you is a pain. Additionally, when your screen is packed to the rafters with targets, it's nearly impossible to keep track of your own five-man squad.

I found the game’s two eras to also be unbalanced, with early game progress on the 40k track much slower and more difficult than Age of Sigmar. Maybe that’s due to a better selection of power-ups in the latter, but I’m not entirely convinced, and I’m certain the game will go through a few rounds of balancing updates after launch to account for it.

I enjoy the way some levels feature environmental mechanics, like tunnels that hide items or elevators to carry you between different map layers. There should be many more of these quirks, as it's strange to wander battlefields peppered with massive turrets in the 40k era while none of them can be used, and 90% of the game's background content is mere set dressing; Vampire Survivors’ own Ode to Castlevania DLC featured a map with much more interactivity.

Speaking of that DLC, Warhammer Survivors starts you off with a similar map function, but this one is pretty much a basic pause menu radar for items. You can zoom in or out to get an idea of where relics and pickups can be found and track them with onscreen indicators, but there’s no landscape detail, nor can you even scrub through the map itself. Since most optional level objectives involve collecting a distant hero or relic, you’re forced to use that shoddy map a lot.

Perhaps most importantly, the game's feedback is far inferior to Vampire Survivors, which may largely be due to the sound. Warhammer Survivors’ audio mixdown is a problem, and I couldn't effectively balance out the SFX and music in settings, eventually opting to silence one or the other. That ultimately wasn't a great loss, as most of the music amounts to heavily-quantized militaristic industrial loops that overstay their welcome fast, though the ambient menu themes are decent enough.

Speaking of menus, the UI in Warhammer Survivors could have done with its own corrective pass (not that Vampire Survivors is much better). Controller input is especially scatterbrained; for instance, pressing A starts a selected level, but doesn't if you're checking off a mod, and you swap worlds with the Start button but then quit the game from the worlds menu with B. This all isn't impossible to manage, but peculiar.

I’ve never understood the fullscreen edge transparency in Vampire, but Warhammer Survivors actually blots out those edges with a skulls texture for some reason. The game’s overhead POV also often works against, as enemies love choking up doorways and walls, which renders them functionally invisible. Player projectiles evaporate on the edges of these surfaces, while enemy shots phase right through. Again, not unmanageable, but this will probably lead to a few frustrating deaths.

The game’s many objectives do dangle carrots aplenty, a boon in any bullet heaven. However, I wish there was a way to index and sort the game's 200+ challenges to the 40 characters they relate to. Additionally, the objectives menu provides no additional info or any explanation of the related rewards, which just seems like a missed opportunity. This could have functioned as its own wiki—like the Bestiarium, which is the best collection of Warhammer lore in the game—but it's just a minimalist list to chew through.

We cut bullet heaven games a lot of slack as a matter of course, and Vampire Survivors is a perfect example. As inspiration to countless others, it’s handily been outplayed at its own game time after time; Brotato shrunk the play space and filed down the progression structure, and Everything is Crab re-expanded that map, evolving the genre’s most basic active/passive upgrade design. Megabonk made traversal equally important to DPS, and Boneraiser Minions used a necromancer concept to present a kind of RTS/autobattler/survivors hybrid. And so on.

Considering these examples, Warhammer Survivors is a few days late and dollars short, albeit at a budget price. For those of you who’ve fully rinsed Vampire Survivors… Well, first off, that’s simply an impressive feat; well done. But secondly, here are another 40 heroes to max out, with hundreds of objectives to clear. Consider your bullet heaven buffet fully restocked.

Warhammer Survivors Isn’t Good Enough to Be a Vampire Survivors Replacement

📅 Nov 10, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Good clones are the sincerest form of flattery

Vampire Survivors and its plethora of clones are always more fun in hour ten than hour one. The passive nature of the auto-attack gameplay means this style of experience lives or dies by how fun and visually over-the-top the action can get once you upgrade your character, gain access to more weapons, and manage to survive long enough to level up or evolve your weapons.

I did eventually hit that point of satisfaction with Warhammer Survivors, which was developed by Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 studio Auroch Digital with help from Vampire Survivors creator Poncle. When I got to the point where I could rip and tear through enemies with a Typhoon Crossbow as followers with upgraded weapons of their own fired at enemies around it, the game offered spectacle worthy of the Warhammer and Survivors names. But getting there doesn’t feel quite as good as its inspiration.

Warhammer Survivors doesn’t contain any sort of important lore to speak of; it’s more of a hodgepodge of various recognizable Warhammer characters (like Boltgun’s Malum Caedo) fighting against waves of unrelenting creatures from both eras of the franchise. Warhammer Survivors is essentially two games in one, with one half based on the sci-fi Warhammer 40,000 and the other on the more fantasy-like Warhammer: Age of Sigmar.

Each half of Warhammer Survivors has unique characters, weapons, enhancements, and objectives to unlock, but the core gameplay loop of each is the same. As a player, all you have to do is walk around levels as your character automatically attacks. Enemies drop experience when they die most of the time, and you collect that to level up and upgrade all of the weapons that you have equipped. Considering Poncle was directly involved with this game, it’s not surprising that Warhammer Survivors does not do much to hide its inspiration or reinvent the formula.

The most unique gimmick here is a follower feature, which solves for the fact that Warhammer Survivors’ characters are connected to factions that only let them use specific weapons. Rather than one character wielding every weapon and upgrading at once, sometimes you can save or summon another character that uses a different weapon to fight alongside you. This feels fitting for the large-scale battles Warhammer is known for. Yet in practice, all it really does is add an additional layer to a choice you were already going to make regardless.

It shouldn’t be too surprising that what you’re getting with this game is Vampire Survivors with a Warhammer coat of paint, even if it does go a bit deeper than Vampire Survivors’ typical crossover DLC. Vampire Survivors is a great game, and Warhammer Survivors is a good one too. That said, I won’t herald Warhammer Survivors as some amazing replacement for that indie classic, because there are some things it doesn’t do quite as well as the original.

Survivors games are all about snowballing power, building up to a chaotic storm of attacks. In Vampire Survivors, almost every weapon has auto aim and will hit something in range when used. But that’s not the case for certain early-game weapons in Warhammer Survivors that shoot the direction the player is facing, like the Boltgun. Those simply don’t mesh well with the auto-attacking gameplay.

The lack of auto-aim on these weapons meant that, as I moved to avoid enemies, I would shoot away from the horde, toward nothing. Eventually, I was able to unlock better weapons that would actually hit the enemies approaching me, but the fact that the earliest weapons are some of the worst means it takes a bit too long to find the fun.

By hour 10 with Vampire Survivors, I had found the characters and weapons I enjoyed using the most. They tended to be the ones that would allow me to exponentially increase in power most smoothly and actually felt like I could survive 20+ minutes and 40+ levels into a single run. From that point onwards, Warhammer Survivors is as good as Vampire Survivorsor any other game of its ilk. It’s just not quite as instantly captivating and rewarding.

Diehard Warhammer fans who haven’t played Vampire Survivors or any of the games it inspired will have a fantastic time with this, but there’s not much reason to abandon the original Vampire Survivors for this official clone. Warhammer Survivors certainly won’t usurp its direct inspiration as my go-to game of this style because it forgets to emulate some of what made Vampire Survivors near-perfect. Still, it confidently delivers exactly what the title promises.

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.
